observation_summary: The BracketingNthOrderBrentSolver fails with a TooManyEvaluationsException because it gets stuck in an infinite loop updating the same side of the bracketing interval, failing to converge on the root.
hypothesis: The solver's rebalancing logic for the bracketing interval is too simplistic. When one side of the bracket ages (exceeds MAXIMAL_AGING), the solver uses a fixed targetY (-REDUCTION_FACTOR * yB) that is insufficient to force the other side to update, leading to an unbalanced interval and excessive evaluations.
prediction: The fix will involve changing the calculation of targetY to be more aggressive or adaptive when aging occurs, likely by incorporating the aging count into the target calculation to force the other side of the bracket to update.
experiment_rationale: The fix diff shows that the simple assignment of targetY was replaced with a weighted calculation involving the aging count (p) and weights (weightA, weightB). This confirms that the original computational strategy for determining the target value was insufficient for rebalancing the interval.
reasoning_summary: The bug is a failure in the computational strategy used to rebalance the bracketing interval. The original code used a static, insufficient formula for targetY, which caused the solver to get stuck. The fix replaces this formula with a more sophisticated, adaptive calculation that accounts for the aging of the brackets. This is a classic algorithmic correction to a procedure that was not correctly handling its state-based rebalancing logic.
evidence_used: The bug report states the solver fails to rebalance the bracketing interval and gets stuck updating the same side.
The fix diff replaces a simple assignment of targetY with a more complex, weighted calculation involving the aging count.
The failing test confirms the solver exceeds the evaluation limit due to this stuck state.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix involves changing an assignment, the root cause is the underlying computational logic (the formula for targetY) that determines how the solver rebalances, which is an algorithmic strategy issue.
There is no missing guard or validation; the logic is executing, but the mathematical strategy for rebalancing is flawed.
